new_statements.quote: 5. Stress is phonemic. Contrastive stress is shown by the following word and phrase pairs: ʔu p'ísi he measured it, ʔu p'isí he wakened him; ʔu c'óni he believed it, ʔu c'oní he shot it; ... ʔu hók'i he dug it out, ʔu hok'í he called him; ... ʔák'əb night, ʔa k'ə́b your hand; čóno a sale, čonó sell it; ʔu lowí he made a hole in it, ʔu lówi he made lots of holes in it. In each of these examples, spoken in the neutral intonational contour, the stressed syllable is higher in pitch than the unstressed syllables. ... Stress shifts occur on some words. The stress may be phonemically on either of two syllables, yielding alternate pronunciations of the same word: tánet or tanét hello.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Keller treats word stress in Tapotzingo Chontal as contrastive (not fixed): it may fall on the final or a non-final syllable and distinguishes otherwise segmentally identical words/verb forms; pitch is raised on the stressed syllable; a few words vary freely between two stress positions, and under emphatic repetition a non-final stress moves to the final syllable. The minimal pairs are mostly morphologically distinct verb forms, and Bennett 2016 (citing Knowles 1984) characterises the contrast as marginal, with stress 'generally predictable on the basis of stem and morpheme boundaries'; Keller & Luciano 1997 likewise show stress tied to particular suffixes (tense suffix stressed, shifting to the root under negation; imperative copy-vowel stressed; Spanish loans final).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Keller 1959 or Keller & Luciano 1997.
new_statements.exceptions: Free variation tánet ~ tanét; loss of stress with vowel loss in sandhi (ʔusubulót < ʔu subí u lót); emphatic/repeat utterances shift non-final stress to the final syllable (ʔákum > ʔakúːm). CONTRADICTING SOURCE: Osorio May 2005 (Tecoluta variety, MA thesis §2.3 p.15) states 'El acento en yokot'an ocurre en la penúltima sílaba' [Stress in Yokot'an falls on the penultimate syllable], with enclitics outside the stress domain (kɨwáne=la); this conflicts with Keller's final-stressed forms (wäyé 'dormir', u yäló 'se cae', čonó) and minimal pairs.
new_statements.domain_note: Keller's examples are words and short clitic+verb phrases in a 'neutral intonational contour'; she explicitly separates stress from question-contour pitch. Proclitic person markers (ʔu, ʔa) are unstressed; Osorio May treats enclitic =la as outside the prosodic word. Variety: Tapotzingo, Nacajuca (Keller); Tecoluta (Osorio May).
new_statements.identity_note: Keller 1959 and Keller & Luciano 1997 describe the Tapotzingo (Nacajuca) variety; Osorio May 2005 describes Tecoluta (also Nacajuca, a neighbouring village); Knowles 1984 (not obtained) describes the San Carlos (Benito Juarez, Macuspana) dialect. All fall under taba1266 (no Glottolog dialect sub-codes).

sources.note: Section 5, p.52: 'Stress is phonemic', with minimal pairs (ʔu p'ísi 'he measured it' vs ʔu p'isí 'he wakened him', ʔák'əb 'night' vs ʔa k'ə́b 'your hand', čóno 'a sale' vs čonó 'sell it', etc.); stressed syllable has higher pitch in neutral contour; some words vary freely (tánet ~ tanét 'hello'); under emphasis/repetition non-final stress shifts to the final syllable (p.53). No default position stated.

sources.note: Survey, §6.1.1 p.496: 'Only one Mayan language shows robust evidence for phonemic stress: in Chontal, minimal pairs like u hok'i [ʔu hˈokʔi] 'he dug it out' and u hok'i [ʔu hokʔˈi] 'he called him' seem to be well-attested (Keller 1959, Knowles 1984, Pérez González 1985). Such contrasts are nonetheless marginal, as stress is generally predictable on the basis of stem and morpheme boundaries.'

sources.note: No general rule; accent is not written in the orthography (p.424). Accent-marked examples show both final (bäcpám, wäyé, u yäló, c'äyé', ajsäcsí') and non-final (sácän 'buscar', c'átä 'solicitada') stress; a~ä alternation depends on stress (p.424); imperative of class-I transitives stresses the copied vowel (chonó, p.452); in negatives 'el acento cambia del sufijo de tiempo a la vocal de la raíz' (yäló vs mach uyál, p.465); Spanish loan verbs keep final stress (p.476).
